references.text: The Samaritan woman had already expressed her surprise that Jesus, a Jewish man, was speaking with her. The disciples' reaction in verse 27 reflects this wonder—it was unusual for a rabbi to converse publicly with a woman ([ref:Joh 4:9|John 4:9]).

After the disciples returned, they changed the subject to food instead of addressing their conversation with the woman. They avoided confronting Jesus with their confusion about the situation ([ref:Joh 4:31-33|John 4:31-33]).

The disciples were often afraid to ask Jesus questions, even when they did not understand what he said or did. In [ref:Luk 9:45|Luke 9:45], they dared not ask him about his words concerning suffering—similarly, no one dared to say "what are you seeking?" or "why are you speaking with her?".
The disciples' reaction—wondering without daring to ask directly—reminds us of the situation at the last meal when they looked at one another in uncertainty ([ref:Joh 13:22|John 13:22]).

In the house of Simon the Pharisee, the host thought to himself that Jesus should know what kind of woman it was who touched him, but he did not say it aloud. The disciples' silent surprise follows a similar pattern—they were amazed by Jesus' interaction with a woman, yet kept it to themselves ([ref:Luk 7:39|Luke 7:39]).

Mark tells us that the disciples did not understand Jesus' words but were afraid to ask him. This is a recurring theme in the Gospels: the disciples are full of questions, yet hold back out of reverence ([ref:Mark 9:32|Mark 9:32]).
